name: TerraPraxis
beneficiaries_note: Our build: a tonne of CO₂ kept out of the air spares people everywhere (heat deaths), so the result is spread by world population; the small air-pollution share, mostly in Asia, is left in the world figure.
summary: TerraPraxis, a US non-profit with a small UK sister company, designs, convenes and builds software to re-power the world's coal plants with advanced nuclear reactors (its REPOWER consortium), and makes the case for advanced nuclear more broadly (the Ten-Terawatt Initiative). This model counts what its 2022-2024 work ($6.3M) adds to two yardsticks, about 4% of the world's suitable coal capacity re-powered with nuclear and a third of the COP28 pledge to triple nuclear capacity, crediting all groups' non-commercial enabling work with 4% of that deployment and TerraPraxis with 8% of that work on coal sites and 0.6% elsewhere. At the defaults a dollar given averts about 0.03 tonnes of CO₂, 0.02 years of healthy life per $1,000. The result is mostly uncertainty: nothing has been built yet, every step from the work to a reactor is a judgment, and the range spans many orders of magnitude; both lines are discounted for missing data.

source.quote: Global coal capacity rose to 2,175 GW, up 259 GW since the Paris Agreement was signed in 2015.

rows.explainer: Coal repowering line. The fleet TerraPraxis's REPOWER work is aimed at: every coal plant in the world, three quarters of them in Asia.

rows.label: Share of coal plant capacity on sites that could host advanced reactors

source.title: US Department of Energy, Office of Nuclear Energy (12 September 2022), Could the nation's coal plant sites help drive a clean energy transition?
source.quote: 80% of the potential sites, with over 250 GW of generating capacity, are suitable for hosting advanced nuclear power plants.

rows.explainer: DOE's national laboratories screened 394 retired and operating US coal sites and found four in five suitable for advanced reactors. No such screening exists for the rest of the world: Asian plants are younger and larger, but many sit in denser or more seismic places. The US share stands in, with the range widened to 50%-90%.

rows.label: Share of the suitable coal capacity re-powered with nuclear heat by about 2050
rows.explainer: A yardstick, not a forecast. In late 2026 no coal plant has been converted anywhere; the first reactor built at a coal site, TerraPower's Natrium plant beside the Naughton coal plant in Wyoming, is under construction for about 2030. On the COP28 pathway to triple nuclear capacity (row below), 4% of the suitable coal capacity, about 70 GW, would be about a tenth of the new reactors. Our judgment, 4% (1% to 12%): reusing a coal site's grid connection and buildings saves 15%-35% of construction cost (DOE 2022), but reactors themselves remain the bottleneck.

rows.label: New capacity the COP28 pledge adds, as a multiple of 2020's capacity

source.title: US Department of Energy (1 December 2023), At COP28, countries launch declaration to triple nuclear energy capacity by 2050
source.quote: advance a global aspirational goal of tripling nuclear energy capacity from 2020 by 2050

rows.explainer: Tripling 2020's capacity means adding twice that much by 2050 (ignoring reactors retired in between, which the built share below absorbs).

rows.label: Advanced nuclear: share of the tripling pathway that gets built
rows.explainer: The pledge is a target (31 countries had signed by 2025), not a forecast. Reference class: the 1970s build wave, when most US orders were cancelled, and recent Western projects (Vogtle, Flamanville, Hinkley Point C) years late and far over budget, against China's steady build and the new pull from data centres. The International Energy Agency's own net-zero analysis, quoted in the declaration, has capacity a little more than doubling rather than tripling. Our judgment, 35% (15% to 70%) of the added capacity.

rows.label: Advanced nuclear: gigawatts built away from coal sites
rows.explainer: The pathway's built capacity less the coal-site reactors already counted in the repowering line, so no reactor is counted twice.

rows.label: Advanced nuclear: tonnes of CO₂ a year those reactors would avert if each replaced coal
rows.explainer: Measured against coal for comparability with the line above; the counterfactual row below says how much cleaner the grid the reactors join is.

rows.label: Share of the deployment due to the period's enabling work (all non-commercial groups together)
rows.explainer: TerraPraxis wins no laws: it designs, convenes and builds tools (standard designs for re-powering a coal plant with Bryden Wood, software with Microsoft, AI licensing tools, the REPOWER consortium of 38 utilities, vendors and financiers, the Ten-Terawatt Initiative). Whether reactors are built turns mostly on cost, finance, demand and policy. Over the 25 years to 2050, the enabling work of all non-commercial groups (national laboratories' studies, the IAEA, EPRI, think tanks, NGOs) might account for a fifth of the deployment, and early years count more than their share: 3 of 25 years at double weight gives about 5%. Our judgment, 4% (1% to 12%), for both lines. A share of a broad trend, not one bet, so no single-event tag.

rows.label: Years the result counts before it would have come anyway
rows.explainer: The site's one answer (docs/normalization.md 2.9): speeding a technology brings its tonnes forward by the shared number of years.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the tonnes are avoided

Expected tonnes a year of the period, before adjustments
rows.explainer: The two lines' expected tonnes, summed and spread over the period's three years.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment: how far the pathway tonnes and the enabling share should be trusted
rows.explainer: The tonnes come from yardsticks (a pledge, a site screening) and judgments, not from a regulator's assessment of a won rule; nuclear projections have run ahead of what was built for fifty years, and that a design or convening programme moves deployment at all is untested. Anchor: our model of Clean Air Task Force takes 0.8 for regulators' estimates of won rules; this is lower because nothing here has been won or measured. Our judgment, 0.7 (0.4 to 1.0), for both lines.

rows.label: Coal repowering: share of coal-site reactors that are extra nuclear, not reactors that would have been built elsewhere
rows.explainer: Much of repowering's value is siting: a reactor at a coal site is cheaper (15%-35% less to build, DOE 2022) and faster to connect, so some reactors move there from other sites rather than being added. The cost saving also makes some reactors happen that otherwise wouldn't, and repowering lets a utility keep its site, staff and grid rights. Our judgment, 40% (15% to 70%) extra.

rows.label: Coal repowering: CO₂ per MWh of the power the extra reactors replace, relative to coal
rows.explainer: Where repowering retires a coal unit early it saves the full coal tonne; where the coal would have closed anyway it saves only what would have replaced it (in the US, about a quarter of coal's CO₂ per MWh: facts: climate.us_coal_replacement_tco2_per_mwh). Repowering is aimed at Asia's young coal fleets, where the alternative to repowering is often more years of coal. Our judgment, 50% (25% to 80%) of a coal MWh's CO₂ in the 2040s.

rows.label: Coal repowering: share of the coal tonnes that are a real cut
rows.explainer: Extra reactors only, each replacing power that emits the share of a coal MWh above.

rows.label: Advanced nuclear: CO₂ per MWh of the power new reactors replace, relative to coal
rows.explainer: New reactors join grids in the late 2030s and 2040s that are cleaner than today's: the world average today is a little under half of a coal MWh's CO₂ and falling as wind and solar grow, faster in Europe and the US than in Asia. Our judgment, 35% (15% to 60%) of coal's tonnes.

rows.label: Coal repowering: TerraPraxis's share of the non-commercial resources behind the enabling work
rows.explainer: TerraPraxis has led coal repowering as an organised idea since 2020 (the REPOWER consortium, standard designs, site-assessment software), on about $2 million a year. Others doing the same kind of work: DOE and its national laboratories (the 2022 coal-to-nuclear study and later site work), the IAEA, EPRI, the Nuclear Innovation Alliance, Clean Air Task Force, the World Nuclear Association, and utilities' own studies; reactor vendors' business development is commercial and sits outside this share. Our judgment, 8% (3% to 20%) of the resources.

rows.label: Advanced nuclear: TerraPraxis's share of the non-commercial resources behind the enabling work
rows.explainer: Its broader advanced nuclear work (the Ten-Terawatt Initiative launched at Davos in January 2025, AI licensing tools with Microsoft, papers on industrial heat and shipping) is a small part of a large field: the Nuclear Energy Institute, Clean Air Task Force's $5 million a year on advanced nuclear, ClearPath, the Breakthrough Institute, Third Way, the World Nuclear Association, the IAEA and the OECD Nuclear Energy Agency, and governments' own deployment programmes. Our judgment, 0.6% (0.2% to 2%).

rows.label: Other work not in the two lines (geothermal, energy modelling), as a share of the modelled value
rows.explainer: Synthetic fuels, industrial heat and shipping are uses of the reactors in the advanced nuclear line. What remains is small: advanced geothermal and energy-system modelling, each a page of the website and a few reports. Their spending is in the cost, so leaving them out would count them as worth nothing. Our judgment, 5% of the modelled value (0 to 15%).

rows.label: Side effect: accident, waste and proliferation risk from more reactors, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Nuclear power's deaths per unit of electricity, accidents and waste included, are about as low as wind's and solar's and far below fossil fuels' (Markandya & Wilkinson 2007). TerraPraxis's tonnes come largely from reactors in Asia and in countries new to nuclear power, where regulators are younger and proliferation worries larger than in the US. Our judgment, −0.5% of the modelled value (−2% to 0).

rows.label: Side effect: jobs and tax revenue kept in coal towns, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: A re-powered plant keeps a coal town's jobs and tax base: DOE's case study counts more than 650 permanent jobs at one converted site. Most of these jobs would exist somewhere else (a reactor built elsewhere, other work), so only the gain from keeping them in place counts, a small amount of income beside the tonnes. Our judgment, +0.3% of the modelled value (0 to 1%).

Share of these tonnes from burning less fossil fuel near people
rows.explainer: Every tonne in both lines is coal or gas power not burned: none is land, capture or methane.

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths per tonne of these fuel tonnes, relative to the fossil-fuel average

source.title: Markandya & Wilkinson (2007), Electricity generation and health, The Lancet 370(9591), 979-990
source.page: Table 2: deaths per TWh from air pollution and accidents, Europe (lignite 32.6, coal 24.6, oil 18.4, gas 2.8)

rows.explainer: The shared rate is 146 air-pollution deaths per million tonnes of fossil CO₂ (climate.deaths_per_tco2e_air_pollution), about 146 deaths per TWh of coal power at a tonne per MWh. European coal killed about 25 per TWh in 2007 (0.17 of the average); US coal plants today about 10 per million tonnes (climate.us_coal_power_smoke_factor, 0.067); Asian coal plants without modern controls far more. The tonnes here come in the late 2030s and 2040s, from grids in Asia, Europe and the US with more pollution controls than today and with gas in the mix. Our judgment around Markandya & Wilkinson's figures, 0.14 of the average (0.04 to 0.35), for both lines.

rows.label: Air pollution these tonnes cut, relative to an average fossil-fuel tonne
rows.explainer: Read by the tco2e unit's conversion (docs/normalization.md 2.5).

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths averted per tonne, counted directly (none here)
rows.explainer: No source counts deaths beside these tonnes; the smoke is in the air-pollution weight above, so nothing is counted twice.

rows.label: Share of these tonnes that are methane
rows.explainer: The tonnes are CO₂ from power plants. Coal not mined also leaks less methane, but no source here sizes it for these plants, and much of the displaced power is not coal: left out, which slightly understates the result.

rows.explainer: Each line's expected tonnes × its own adjustments, summed and spread over the period's three years, with the other work and the side effects added as shares.
